content: Powdery mildew (Erysiphe necator) is the most common grape disease. Symptoms: white powdery coating on leaves, shoots, and berries. Causes berry cracking and yield loss. Treatment: sulfur-based fungicides every 7-14 days, potassium bicarbonate, or neem oil. Prevention: good air circulation, avoid overhead irrigation, resistant varieties like Regent or Chambourcin. Most severe in warm dry days with cool nights.

Downy mildew (Plasmopara viticola) thrives in wet, humid conditions. Symptoms: oily yellow spots on upper leaf surface, white fluffy growth underneath. Can destroy entire crop. Treatment: copper-based fungicides, mancozeb. Prevention: spray before rain, improve canopy airflow, avoid wetting foliage. Worst after heavy rainfall in spring.

Botrytis cinerea (gray mold) infects berries, especially in tight clusters. Symptoms: gray fuzzy mold on berries, berries shrivel and collapse. Thrives in cool, wet weather near harvest. Treatment: iprodione, fenhexamid fungicides. Prevention: open canopy for airflow, leaf removal around clusters, avoid excess nitrogen, harvest before heavy rains.

Phylloxera (Daktulosphaira vitifoliae) is the most destructive grape pest. It feeds on roots causing galls and vine death. No cure once infected. Prevention: plant on phylloxera-resistant rootstocks (SO4, 3309C, 101-14). Grafted vines are standard protection. Sandy soils provide some natural resistance. Do not move soil or equipment from infested vineyards.

Grape berry moth (Paralobesia viteana) larvae bore into berries causing direct damage and secondary fungal infections. Three generations per year. Symptoms: webbing around berry clusters, entry holes, berry shriveling. Treatment: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) for organic control, or spinosad, carbaryl. Monitor with pheromone traps to time sprays accurately.

Two-spotted spider mites and grape rust mites cause stippling and bronzing of leaves, reducing photosynthesis. Worst in hot dry summers. Treatment: insecticidal soap, neem oil, sulfur sprays, or miticides like bifenazate. Predatory mites (Phytoseiidae) are excellent biological control. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill beneficial predators.

Prune during dormancy (after leaf fall, before bud break) when vines are fully dormant. Spur pruning: leave 2-3 node spurs on permanent cordon arms — best for table grapes and some wine varieties. Cane pruning: replace entire fruiting wood each year with 10-15 node canes — best for Pinot Noir, Riesling. Remove 80-90% of previous year's growth. Always cut to healthy wood (green inside).

Grapevines are drought-tolerant but need consistent moisture for quality fruit. Drip irrigation is most efficient — deliver 1-2 gallons per vine per day during growing season. Deficit irrigation (slight water stress) after fruit set improves berry quality and concentration. Avoid irrigation 2-3 weeks before harvest to concentrate sugars. Sandy soils need more frequent watering than clay soils.

Grapevines need balanced nutrition. Nitrogen: apply 30-50 lbs/acre in spring, avoid excess (causes excessive vigor, disease). Potassium: critical for fruit quality and cold hardiness — apply based on soil test. Phosphorus: rarely deficient in established vineyards. Leaf tissue testing in July is the best way to assess nutrition. Compost and cover crops improve soil health and reduce fertilizer needs.

Harvest timing depends on grape variety and intended use. Measure Brix (sugar content) with a refractometer: table grapes 16-20 Brix, wine grapes 20-26 Brix depending on style. Also check: pH (3.2-3.6 for wine), titratable acidity, seed color (brown = ripe), berry flavor. Taste is the most important indicator. Harvest in cool morning hours to preserve freshness and aroma.

Spring frosts after bud break are the biggest weather risk for grapes. Methods: wind machines (mix warm air from above), overhead sprinklers (ice forms but releases heat protecting buds), smudge pots, site selection on slopes above frost pockets. Delay pruning to delay bud break in frost-prone areas. Varieties with late bud break (Chardonnay, Cabernet) are more frost-tolerant than early varieties (Chardonnay).

Good canopy management reduces disease pressure and improves fruit quality. Shoot thinning: remove excess shoots early (2-4 weeks after bud break) to 3-6 shoots per foot of cordon. Leaf removal: remove 2-4 leaves around clusters to improve airflow and light exposure — do after berry set. Hedging: trim shoot tips to control excessive vigor. VSP (Vertical Shoot Positioning) trellis is most common.

Best grape varieties for hot climates: Grenache, Syrah, Tempranillo, Mourvedre, Zinfandel (wine); Muscat of Alexandria, Thompson Seedless, Flame Seedless (table). These varieties tolerate heat, drought, and high sugar accumulation. Plant on south-facing slopes, use deficit irrigation, harvest at night or early morning. Avoid thin-skinned varieties like Pinot Noir in extreme heat.

Cold-hardy varieties for northern climates: Marquette, Frontenac, La Crescent, Itasca, Crimson Pearl. These survive -30°F (-34°C) and are bred for short growing seasons. For milder cold regions: Riesling, Gewurztraminer, Pinot Noir, Regent. Protect vines by hilling soil over graft union in fall, using mulch, and burying canes in extreme climates.

Grapes prefer well-drained soils with pH 5.5-6.5. Avoid waterlogged or compacted soils. Before planting: test soil pH and nutrients, add lime to raise pH or sulfur to lower it, deep rip compacted soils (18-24 inches), install drainage if needed. Grapes grow well in poor, rocky soils — too fertile causes excessive growth. Choose rootstock based on soil type, phylloxera risk, and vigor needed.

Spray early morning or late evening when thrips are active on leaf undersides. Use a high spray volume (1000–1500 L/ha) to ensure thorough coverage of lower leaf surfaces and berry cups. Rotate between IRAC 5 (Spinosad), IRAC 6 (Emamectin), and IRAC 28 (Cyantraniliprole) to manage resistance—thrips develop resistance rapidly to pyrethroids and organophosphates. Avoid repeated use of IRAC 4A (neonicotinoids) as cross-resistance is common. Maintain a PHI of 3–7 days for Spinosad; REI is 12 hours. Integrate with blue sticky traps for monitoring. Never spray during bloom to protect pollinators. Category: Insect (Thrips). Key registered chemicals: Spinosad 45% SC, Emamectin benzoate 5% SG, Fipronil 5% SC, Imidacloprid 17.8% SL. Critical spray timing: Early season (bud burst to pre-bloom); target 1st & 2nd instar nymphs..

Scirtothrips cause severe berry russeting and leaf bronzing; economic thresholds are extremely low (1–2 per leaf). Use IRAC 5 (Spinetoram) or IRAC 4C (Sulfoxaflor) for quick knock-down, followed by IRAC 28 (Cyantraniliprole) for residual activity. Because they feed on meristematic tissues, translaminar products (like Cyantraniliprole) are superior to contact-only sprays. Rotate MOA every application—do not spray same group twice consecutively. Monitor with white sticky traps. Avoid tank-mixing with alkaline products. PHI: 3–7 days. Consider predatory mites (Amblyseius) as biological control; avoid broad-spectrum pyrethroids which flare mite populations. Category: Insect (Thrips). Key registered chemicals: Spinetoram 11.7% SC, Sulfoxaflor 21.8% SC, Cyantraniliprole 10.26% OD. Critical spray timing: Pre-bloom to berry set; spray when 2–3 thrips per leaf are observed..

The most critical spray is the “bud-burst” application just as buds begin to swell—this targets overwintering adults emerging from soil/leaf litter. Use IRAC 3A (Cypermethrin/Deltamethrin) for rapid adult knock-down. Follow up 7 days later with IRAC 1B (Acephate) if pressure persists, but observe the 66-day PHI for Acephate if used later in the season. Since beetles are large, ensure coarse droplets for canopy penetration. After fruit set, only spray if >10% of new shoots show feeding damage. Protect natural enemies (ground beetles) by spot-treating only the borders. PHI for pyrethroids: 7–14 days. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Beetle (Coleoptera). Key registered chemicals: Cypermethrin 25% EC, Deltamethrin 2.8% EC, Acephate 75% SP. Critical spray timing: Bud swell stage (dormant to bud break); target overwintering adults..

Foliar sprays are largely ineffective against the larval stage inside shoots. Management relies on prophylactic trunk painting using Chlorpyrifos + fungicidal paste during the adult emergence period (pre-monsoon). For severe infestations, apply Fipronil 5% SC as a soil drench around the root zone to target neonate larvae before they bore. Remove and destroy girdled, wilting shoots immediately—this is the single most effective cultural practice. Monitor adults using light traps during peak emergence. Rotate trunk paints with Deltamethrin to avoid resistance. PHI for soil drenches is 60+ days; do not apply near harvest. REI: 24–48 hours. Category: Beetle (Cerambycid). Key registered chemicals: Chlorpyrifos 50% EC, Fipronil 5% SC (soil drench), Deltamethrin (trunk paint). Critical spray timing: Adult emergence (May–June) and egg-laying period..

Target the first-instar crawlers as they are the most vulnerable. Use IGRs (Buprofezin/Pyriproxyfen) at peak crawler emergence for excellent ovicidal/nymphal activity. For systemic action, apply Spirotetramat which moves both acropetally and basipetally, protecting new growth and hidden colonies under bark. Control ants (Pheidole spp.) aggressively—they protect mealybugs from predators; use ant baits containing Fipronil or Propoxur. Add a spreader-sticker to penetrate waxy secretions. Rotate IRAC 23 with 16/7C to manage resistance. PHI ranges 7–14 days. Release Cryptolaemus montrouzieri (ladybird beetle) when populations are low. Category: Sap-sucking insect (Hemiptera). Key registered chemicals: Buprofezin 25% SC (IRAC 16), Pyriproxyfen 10% EC (IRAC 7C), Spirotetramat 15.31% OD (IRAC 23), Imidacloprid 17.8% SL (IRAC 4A). Critical spray timing: Crawler emergence (spring & post-monsoon); pre-bloom and post-veraison..

Phenacoccus is highly polyphagous and breeds rapidly under warm conditions. Since they hide in leaf axils and between bunches, use systemic/translaminar insecticides—Spirotetramat is the gold standard as it prevents egg hatch and suppresses oviposition in adults. For quick suppression, mix with Sulfoxaflor (IRAC 4C) to overcome neonicotinoid resistance. Thorough coverage with a high-volume spray (1500 L/ha) is mandatory to reach hidden colonies. Always combine with a wetting agent to break the waxy cottony covering. Rotate IRAC 23 → 4C → 16. PHI: 7 days. Encourage parasitoid wasps (Aenasius bambawalei) by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays. REI: 12 hours. Category: Sap-sucking insect (Hemiptera). Key registered chemicals: Buprofezin 25% SC, Spirotetramat 15.31% OD, Sulfoxaflor 21.8% SC. Critical spray timing: Early infestation stage; pre-flowering to berry setting..

Dormant oil sprays (2–3% petroleum oil) are the most effective, environmentally safe option—apply immediately after pruning to smother overwintering scales. If crawlers are detected in spring using double-sided sticky tape on canes, apply Pyriproxyfen (IRAC 7C) which acts as a juvenile hormone mimic, preventing metamorphosis. Scale insects are notoriously resistant to OPs; avoid repeated Chlorpyrifos. For severe infestations, Spray oil + Buprofezin tank-mix provides excellent synergistic control. Ensure complete coverage of all bark crevices. PHI for oils: 0 days (safe near harvest). REI: 24 hours for oils. Biological control: Coccophagus wasps are effective if broad-spectrum sprays are avoided. Category: Scale insect (Hemiptera). Key registered chemicals: Mineral oil (dormant), Chlorpyrifos 50% EC, Pyriproxyfen 10% EC. Critical spray timing: Dormant season (post-pruning) and crawler emergence (spring)..

Aphids are typically secondary pests flared by broad-spectrum insecticides. Use soft chemicals: Flonicamid and Pymetrozine are highly selective, killing feeding aphids while sparing predators like ladybirds and lacewings. For organic vineyards, Azadirachtin (neem) acts as an antifeedant and growth regulator—apply at 7–10 day intervals. Since aphids reproduce parthenogenically, resistance to neonicotinoids (IRAC 4A) is widespread; avoid them. Spray when colonies are localized; spot treatment prevents widespread resistance. Focus on undersides of young leaves. PHI: 3–7 days. REI: 12 hours. Wash off honeydew with water jets to reduce sooty mold. Category: Sap-sucking insect (Hemiptera). Key registered chemicals: Flonicamid 50% WG (IRAC 9C), Pymetrozine 50% WG (IRAC 9B), Azadirachtin 1% EC. Critical spray timing: Early season; when colonies are first observed on young shoots/leaves..

Whiteflies cause direct damage via sap-sucking and indirect damage via sooty mold from honeydew. Their cryptic nymphal stages on lower leaf surfaces require translaminar or systemic products. Spirotetramat provides excellent suppression of both nymphs and adults while being safe to most beneficials. IGRs (Buprofezin/Pyriproxyfen) are brilliant for nymphal control but have no adult activity—combine with a quick-knockdown adulticide like Sulfoxaflor (IRAC 4C) if adults are swarming. Do not rely solely on neonicotinoids (resistance documented globally). Apply high-volume sprays targeting the abaxial leaf surfaces. PHI: 7–14 days. Use yellow sticky traps for monitoring and to mass-trap adults. Category: Sap-sucking insect (Hemiptera). Key registered chemicals: Buprofezin 25% SC (IRAC 16), Pyriproxyfen 10% EC (IRAC 7C), Spirotetramat 15.31% OD (IRAC 23), Imidacloprid (IRAC 4A). Critical spray timing: Early morning when adults are less active; target nymphal stages..

Leafhoppers cause “hopperburn” – chlorotic stippling that reduces photosynthesis. Monitor using yellow sticky traps and sweep nets. The economic threshold is 10–15 nymphs per leaf. Sulfoxaflor provides rapid, long-lasting control with low impact on predators compared to pyrethroids. Rotate with IRAC 1B (Acephate) but respect the 66-day PHI for grapes—do not use Acephate after flowering if harvest is early. If using Bifenthrin (IRAC 3A), limit to one application per season to avoid mite flaring. Apply sprays when nymphs are present (they are easier to kill than adults). Ensure penetration into the mid-canopy where nymphs reside. PHI: 7–14 days. Category: Leafhopper (Hemiptera). Key registered chemicals: Acephate 75% SP (IRAC 1B), Imidacloprid (IRAC 4A), Sulfoxaflor (IRAC 4C), Bifenthrin 10% EC (IRAC 3A). Critical spray timing: Nymph emergence (spring); pre-bloom to post-bloom..

Tree crickets chew circular holes in leaves and damage tender shoots but are usually minor pests in grapes. Their nocturnal feeding habits make them difficult to target. Apply pyrethroid (IRAC 3A) sprays in the late evening if severe localized damage occurs (>20% leaf damage). Because they prefer field borders, spot-spraying affected perimeter rows is sufficient and reduces ecological disruption. Combine with sanitation—remove tall weeds/grasses near the vineyard that harbor adults. No specific PHI concerns for pyrethroids (7–14 days). Avoid spraying if beneficial insect activity is high, as tree crickets rarely reach economic thresholds in managed vineyards. Use light traps to monitor adult emergence. Category: Chewing insect (Orthoptera). Key registered chemicals: Cypermethrin 25% EC, Deltamethrin 2.8% EC. Critical spray timing: Nighttime during pre-bloom / early shoot growth..

Spodoptera is a voracious defoliator and cluster feeder. NPV (Nuclear Polyhedrosis Virus) is highly effective on 1st–2nd instar larvae and is completely safe for natural enemies—apply at 1×10⁹ POB/mL; requires cool, shaded conditions. For chemical control, use Emamectin benzoate (IRAC 6) or Chlorantraniliprole (IRAC 28) which have translaminar activity and residual control. Resistance to pyrethroids and OPs is widespread, so avoid IRAC 3A/1B for this pest. Spray during early morning when larvae are actively feeding. If spraying NPV, avoid UV exposure (apply in evening). PHI: 7 days. Always rotate IRAC 28 ↔ 6 ↔ 5 to prevent resistance. Category: Caterpillar (Lepidoptera). Key registered chemicals: Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC (IRAC 28), Emamectin benzoate 5% SG (IRAC 6), Spinosad 45% SC (IRAC 5), NPV (0.43% AS). Critical spray timing: Early instar larvae (1st–3rd instar); avoid late instars..

Leaf folders create “nests” by folding leaves with silk, protecting them from contact sprays. Thus, translaminar/systemic insecticides (IRAC 28) are superior to contact pyrethroids. Apply Chlorantraniliprole at the first sign of larval webbing; it penetrates leaf tissues to reach feeding larvae inside folds. For organic or soft programs, Spinosad (IRAC 5) is moderately effective if applied with a wetting agent and at high volume to force penetration into folds. Pruning off folded leaves during winter reduces overwintering pupae. Monitor with pheromone traps. Rotate IRAC 28 with IRAC 5. PHI: 7 days. REI: 12 hours. Category: Caterpillar (Lepidoptera). Key registered chemicals: Spinosad 45% SC (IRAC 5), Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC (IRAC 28), Lambda-cyhalothrin 5% EC (IRAC 3A). Critical spray timing: Pre-monsoon / early monsoon; target 1st generation larvae..

Helicoverpa larvae bore directly into berries, causing internal rot and dropping. NPV (HaNPV) is the safest option—apply at 1×10⁹ POB/mL at 7-day intervals starting at 50% flowering; it works best on neonates. For chemical control, Indoxacarb (IRAC 22A) and Emamectin (IRAC 6) are highly effective with ovicidal/larvicidal activity. Resistance to pyrethroids and OPs is extreme—do not waste resources on IRAC 3A/1B. Use pheromone traps (20/ha) to monitor adult flight; spray when traps catch >5 moths/trap/night. Always rotate IRAC 22A ↔ 6 ↔ 28. PHI: 7 days. Apply in the late evening to protect pollinators. Category: Caterpillar (Lepidoptera). Key registered chemicals: Emamectin benzoate 5% SG (IRAC 6), Indoxacarb 14.5% SC (IRAC 22A), Chlorantraniliprole (IRAC 28), NPV (0.43% AS). Critical spray timing: Egg-laying period (flowering to berry enlargement)..

This is the most damaging berry pest in grapes. Target 1st generation during pre-bloom to break the cycle—this prevents the 2nd and 3rd generations from causing direct berry webbing and rot. Use Chlorantraniliprole (IRAC 28) at 50% bloom for long residual protection. For organic/soft programs, Spinosad or Bt are effective if applied exactly at egg hatch (monitor degree days). Pheromone confusion (mating disruption) is highly effective—install 500 dispensers/ha before the first adult emergence. Rotate IRAC 28 ↔ 5 ↔ 6 strictly. Do not use pyrethroids during flowering (bee toxicity). PHI: 3–7 days. REI: 4–12 hours. Category: Moth (Lepidoptera). Key registered chemicals: Spinosad 45% SC (IRAC 5), Chlorantraniliprole 18.5% SC (IRAC 28), Emamectin benzoate 5% SG (IRAC 6). Critical spray timing: Critical: Pre-bloom (1st gen), Post-bloom (2nd gen), Veraison (3rd gen)..

Larvae tunnel deep into the main trunk, making foliar sprays useless. Prophylactic trunk painting with Chlorpyrifos + copper paste immediately after pruning is mandatory in endemic regions. For active infestations, inject Fipronil + solvent into the bore holes using a syringe, then seal with clay. Adult beetles are nocturnal and can be mass-trapped using light traps during the pre-monsoon period. Sanitation is critical: remove and burn dead/severely infested vines to reduce source population. There are no effective biological controls for borers; rely on cultural and chemical prophylaxis. PHI for trunk applications is not relevant for fruit, but follow REI of 24–48 hours for handling. Category: Beetle (Cerambycid). Key registered chemicals: Chlorpyrifos 50% EC (trunk paste), Fipronil 5% SC (soil), Deltamethrin (trunk spray). Critical spray timing: Adult emergence (summer monsoon); prophylactic treatments..

Shot hole borers are attracted to stressed, weakened vines (drought, mechanical damage). Management is primarily preventive: maintain vigorous vine health and avoid water stress. Azadirachtin can be applied as a trunk repellent to deter boring beetles. For chemical control, Chlorpyrifos trunk sprays during adult flight periods (monitor with ethanol-baited traps) can reduce attacks. Fungal symbionts carried by the beetles cause the real damage (ambrosia fungi); applying Trichoderma to pruning wounds can outcompete the ambrosia fungi. Remove and chip infested wood immediately—do not leave in the vineyard. PHI for trunk sprays is not applicable. Promote predatory beetles by avoiding general insecticides. Category: Beetle (Scolytine). Key registered chemicals: Azadirachtin 1% EC (repellent), Chlorpyrifos 50% EC (trunk spray), Metarhizium anisopliae (bio). Critical spray timing: When stress conditions occur; early season..

Mites flare up dramatically after pyrethroid/organophosphate applications (which kill their natural predators). Use IRAC 10B (Etoxazole) or IRAC 20D (Bifenazate) which are ovicidal and safe to adults of beneficials. Abamectin (IRAC 6) provides rapid knock-down of motile stages but does not kill eggs—must be followed up 7 days later with an ovicide. Rotate MOA every spray (21A → 10B → 6 → 23) to prevent the rapid resistance typical of spider mites. Always include a non-ionic wetter to improve contact. Apply high-pressure spray covering undersides of leaves. PHI: 3–7 days. REI: 12 hours. Use predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) to suppress colonies biologically. Category: Mite (Acari). Key registered chemicals: Abamectin 1.9% EC (IRAC 6), Fenpyroximate 5% SC (IRAC 21A), Etoxazole 10% SC (IRAC 10B), Sulphur 80% WG. Critical spray timing: Hot, dry spells (March–June); early detection at 5–10 mites/leaf..

Same management as Red Spider Mite, but note that Two-spotted mite thrives in dusty conditions. Reduce dust via gravel mulches or irrigation. Spiromesifen (IRAC 23) offers excellent suppression of all life stages and has a gentle effect on predatory mites. Do not use Sulphur when temperatures exceed 32°C—causes severe phytotoxicity (leaf burn). In table grapes, zero tolerance for mite damage to rachis/berries; apply Cyflumetofen (IRAC 25) for quick knockdown before harvest (PHI 3 days). Maintain 100% coverage; mites hide in the berry cluster zone. Alternate chemistries religiously. Category: Mite (Acari). Key registered chemicals: Same as Red Spider Mite.. Critical spray timing: Same as above..

Yellow mites are typically a spring pest before the hot summer, unlike spider mites. They feed on lower leaf surfaces causing yellow stippling. Hexythiazox (IRAC 10A) is excellent as a preventive ovicide applied when mite density is low. For curative control, Bifenazate (IRAC 20D) provides rapid mortality of adult females and has a very short PHI (3 days), suitable for the pre-harvest window. Propargite (IRAC 12C) is a strong, cheap miticide but is phytotoxic to certain table grape varieties—test on a small patch first. Do not apply sulfur if using oil-based miticides. Rotate 10A → 20D → 12C. PHI: 3–14 days. Category: Mite (Acari). Key registered chemicals: Hexythiazox 5.45% EC (IRAC 10A), Bifenazate 22.6% SC (IRAC 20D), Propargite 57% EC (IRAC 12C). Critical spray timing: Early season (spring) on lower leaves; warm spells..

Rust mites are extremely small (invisible to naked eye) and cause leaf bronzing/rusting and shoot distortion. Early detection via 10x hand lens is crucial. Sulphur is the most cost-effective and standard treatment—apply at 3–5 kg/ha during bud break. For severe infestation, Abamectin (IRAC 6) is highly effective and translaminar, reaching mites in curled leaves. Because they are eriophyids, avoid pyrethroids which flare them. A single well-timed spray at 70% bud break often prevents the entire season's damage. PHI for Sulphur: 7–14 days. Do not apply sulfur above 30°C. Consider dormant oil sprays to kill overwintering females in bark crevices. Category: Eriophyid Mite (Acari). Key registered chemicals: Sulphur 80% WG, Abamectin 1.9% EC, Fenpyroximate 5% SC. Critical spray timing: Bud burst to early shoot growth (spring)..

Bud mites cause “big bud” galls and severely reduce primary shoots. Management must occur before buds swell. Apply dormant Sulphur + oil immediately after pruning to kill overwintering mites inside bud scales. If missed, a green-tip spray of Abamectin (IRAC 6) is essential—it penetrates the bud scales to target mites as they emerge. In susceptible varieties, two applications may be required (dormant + green-tip). Infested galled buds should be pruned and destroyed—do not leave them on the ground. Rotating Abamectin with Fenpyroximate helps manage potential resistance. PHI: 7–14 days. This pest demands 100% coverage of all spurs and canes during the dormant application. Category: Eriophyid Mite (Acari). Key registered chemicals: Sulphur 80% WG (dormant/late), Abamectin 1.9% EC, Fenpyroximate 5% SC. Critical spray timing: Dormant season (post-pruning) and green tip stage..

Nematodes cause root galling, stunting, and wilting—management is difficult post-infection. Pre-plant soil fumigation is the ideal practice. For established vineyards, apply Fluopyram or Fluensulfone as a soil drench during the active root-growth phase (spring/monsoon). These newer nematicides have low phytotoxicity compared to carbofuran. Fluensulfone 2% GR should be incorporated into the drip-irrigation zone—it provides 60–90 days of control. Cyclobutrifluoram is a seed treatment (for rootstocks) but can be applied to vine basal soil. Rotate with organic amendments like neem cake or Paecilomyces lilacinus (bio-nematicide from the list) to build soil suppressiveness. PHI: 30+ days. Category: Nematode. Key registered chemicals: Fluopyram 34.48% SC (IRAC/Nematicide), Fluensulfone 2% GR, Cyclobutrifluoram 41.6% FS. Critical spray timing: Pre-planting (soil fumigation) or early post-plant (soil drench)..

Citrus nematode is a semi-endoparasite that damages feeder roots in sandy/loamy soils. Management mirrors Root-knot nematode. Fluopyram (IRAC 7 - SDHI fungicide/nematicide) has good activity; apply as a post-plant drench to the dripline. Bio-nematicides (like P. lilacinus) are excellent for organic/integrated control—apply 2.5–5 kg/ha mixed with well-decomposed FYM (Farm Yard Manure) to enhance colonization. Soil solarization during hot summers is highly effective if done pre-plant. Maintain healthy vine vigor; foliar nutrition (Zn, Fe) can mask symptoms but does not reduce nematode populations. Rotate chemical nematicides to avoid resistance. PHI: 14–30 days. Category: Nematode. Key registered chemicals: Fluopyram 34.48% SC, Paecilomyces lilacinus 1.15% WP (bio). Critical spray timing: Pre-planting or early root flush..

Reniform nematode is sedentary and causes severe stunting in light-textured soils. Since they primarily affect young vines, focus on rootstock selection (resistant varieties) and pre-plant soil treatment. For established vines showing decline, apply Fluensulfone as a drip-chemigation treatment—it moves through the soil profile to the root zone. Depth of placement is critical—nematodes are in the 15–30 cm root zone; inject soil drenches at least 5 cm deep. Combine with organic matter (compost) to encourage nematode-antagonistic microflora. Avoid repeated application of the same chemical; rotate Fluopyram with Fluensulfone. PHI: 30 days. REI: 48 hours for handling granules. Category: Nematode. Key registered chemicals: Fluensulfone 2% GR, Fluopyram 34.48% SC, Cyclobutrifluoram 41.6% FS. Critical spray timing: Soil application at root flush (pre-monsoon)..

Snails are major pests during wet, humid weather, feeding on leaves and causing direct berry damage near harvest. Metaldehyde baits are the standard—apply 2–3 kg/ha in the evening before expected rainfall. Do not apply baits directly on the ground if immediate rain is expected (>5 mm washes them away). Use bait traps (citrus rinds or beer traps) to monitor activity. Remove weeds and debris (refuge sites) to make the vineyard less hospitable. Copper sulphate sprays (1% solution) on trunks acts as a repellent barrier. Metaldehyde PHI: 7 days. REI: 12 hours. Avoid bait application if pets/livestock roam the vineyard (toxicity risks). Category: Mollusc. Key registered chemicals: Metaldehyde 2.5% DP (Granules/Bait). Critical spray timing: Post-rainfall periods; early morning/late evening when active..

Slugs cause irregular holes in leaves and etchings on berry skin, especially on low-hanging clusters near the ground. Metaldehyde baits are effective, but repeated application is needed because slugs are continuous breeders in wet conditions. Apply baits in the early morning when they are most active. To protect clusters, consider training vines higher on the trellis and removing lower leaves. Copper barriers (copper hydroxide paint) around trunk bases are an excellent non-chemical deterrent—copper reacts with slug slime causing a repellent shock. Sanitation (removing leaf litter) is crucial. PHI: 7 days. Do not over-apply Metaldehyde if water sources are nearby (toxic to aquatic life). Category: Mollusc. Key registered chemicals: Metaldehyde 2.5% DP, Copper Hydroxide 50% WP (barrier). Critical spray timing: Monsoon/wet periods; early morning or twilight..

Birds cause 10–40% crop loss in unprotected vineyards. Physical exclusion nets (20–25mm mesh) draped directly over the canopy are the only reliable long-term method—install 2–3 weeks before veraison. Reflective tapes, helium balloons with predator eyes, and regular shooting (licensed) are short-term deterrents. Rotate scare devices daily to prevent habituation. Chemical repellents (like anthraquinone) are not on this specific list but may be available locally; they require frequent reapplication after rain. Harvest early if heavy pressure is expected. Net costs are high but amortized over vine life; they also protect against hailstorms. Category: Vertebrate. Key registered chemicals: Physical nets, acoustic/scare devices (No chemical registered in this list for birds). Critical spray timing: Veraison (berry coloring) to harvest..

Fruit bats feed exclusively at night, ripping clusters and scattering berries. Monofilament nylon netting (30mm mesh) draped over the trellis is highly effective. Because bats are protected wildlife in many regions, poisoning is illegal and discouraged. Use acoustic deterrents (ultrasonic devices) combined with solar-powered flashing lights to disturb feeding. Harvest as early as possible in the morning to remove the attractant. Prune to keep clusters visible but avoid leaving netting loose (bats can entangle). Ensure nets are secured at the bottom to prevent bats from climbing underneath. Cultural practice: maintain alternate fruit trees away from the vineyard to divert attention. Category: Mammal (Vertebrate). Key registered chemicals: Physical nets (birds), sound deterrents (No chemical registered). Critical spray timing: Veraison to harvest (nighttime feeding)..

Rodents gnaw roots, girdle trunks at ground level, and feed on ripening berries. Zinc Phosphide (80%) is an acute toxicant—prepare fresh bait with moistened grain and place it inside secure bait stations to prevent non-target wildlife access; one application is usually sufficient. For chronic anticoagulants, use Brodifacoum blocks—they are highly lethal in a single feeding. Baiting should be strictly done during dormancy (winter) to avoid poison bait being dragged into clusters. Sanitation (removing piles of pruned wood, controlling weeds) eliminates rodent habitat. Place bait stations 10–15 meters apart along the vineyard borders. REI: 48 hours. PHI: Not applicable for baiting, but do not place near harvest. Category: Mammal (Vertebrate). Key registered chemicals: Zinc Phosphide 80% Powder (bait), Brodifacoum 0.005% BB, Bromadiolone 0.005% RB. Critical spray timing: Pre-planting and early season; baiting during dormancy..

Spinosad (45% SC) is used against Grapevine Thrips (Rhipiphorothrips cruentatus). IRAC Group 5, mode of action: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor allosteric modulator (Contact / Stomach). Critical crop stage: Pre-bloom to berry set. Spray timing: 1st–2nd instar nymphs on leaf undersides; apply early morning/evening. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 3 days, REI: 4 hrs. Resistance risk: Low-Medium. Rotate with IRAC groups: 28, 6, 4C. Pollinator safety: Moderate (low toxicity when dry). Beneficial impact: Low (target-specific).

Spinetoram (11.7% SC) is used against Scirtothrips (Scirtothrips dorsalis). IRAC Group 5, mode of action: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor allosteric modulator (Contact / Stomach). Critical crop stage: Pre-bloom to berry set. Spray timing: When 2–3 thrips/leaf observed; target early instars. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 3 days, REI: 4 hrs. Resistance risk: Low-Medium. Rotate with IRAC groups: 28, 4C, 22A. Pollinator safety: Moderate. Beneficial impact: Low.

Cypermethrin (25% EC) is used against Grapevine Flea Beetle (Scelodonta strigicollis). IRAC Group 3A, mode of action: Sodium channel modulator (Contact). Critical crop stage: Dormant to bud swell. Spray timing: Spray at bud-burst when adults emerge from soil/litter; focus on canes. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Medium. Rotate with IRAC groups: 1B, 28. Pollinator safety: High Toxicity. Beneficial impact: High Impact.

Chlorpyrifos (50% EC) [Trunk paint] is used against Stem Girdler (Sthenias grisator). IRAC Group 1B, mode of action: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor (Contact / Stomach). Critical crop stage: Adult emergence (pre-monsoon). Spray timing: Apply as trunk paint/paste to prevent egg-laying; remove girdled shoots. Rainfastness: 4–6 hrs. PHI: N/A (trunk) days, REI: 24 hrs. Resistance risk: Medium. Rotate with IRAC groups: 3A (sprays). Pollinator safety: High Toxicity. Beneficial impact: High Impact.

Spirotetramat (15.31% OD) is used against Mealybug (Planococcus ficus, Maconellicoccus hirsutus). IRAC Group 23, mode of action: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase inhibitor (Systemic (bi-directional)). Critical crop stage: Peak crawler emergence (spring & post-monsoon). Spray timing: Apply when crawlers active; ensure coverage of bark crevices & axils. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: 16, 7C, 4C. Pollinator safety: Moderate. Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Sulfoxaflor (21.8% SC) is used against Cottony Mealybug (Phenacoccus solenopsis). IRAC Group 4C, mode of action: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist (sulfoximine) (Systemic / Contact). Critical crop stage: Early infestation (pre-flowering). Spray timing: Apply when localized colonies spotted; combine with wetting agent for waxy cover. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Medium. Rotate with IRAC groups: 23, 16, 7C. Pollinator safety: High Toxicity. Beneficial impact: High Impact.

Pyriproxyfen (10% EC) is used against Grapevine Scale Insect (Parthenolecanium spp.). IRAC Group 7C, mode of action: Juvenile hormone mimic (Contact / Stomach). Critical crop stage: Dormant season & spring crawler emergence. Spray timing: Apply dormant oil post-pruning; follow with IGR at crawler peak (sticky tape monitoring). Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: 16, 23, 4C. Pollinator safety: Moderate. Beneficial impact: Low (safe to adults).

Flonicamid (50% WG) is used against Aphids (Aphis gossypii, Myzus persicae). IRAC Group 9C, mode of action: Chordotonal organ TRPV channel modulator (Systemic (anti-feedant)). Critical crop stage: Early season (shoot growth). Spray timing: Spray when colonies first appear on young leaves/undersides. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 3 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: 9B, 4C, 23. Pollinator safety: Moderate. Beneficial impact: Low.

Buprofezin (25% SC) is used against Whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci). IRAC Group 16, mode of action: Chitin synthesis inhibitor (Contact (nymphal)). Critical crop stage: Nymphal emergence (spring/summer). Spray timing: Target early instars on lower leaf surfaces; combine with adulticide if swarm. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: 23, 7C, 4C. Pollinator safety: Moderate. Beneficial impact: Low (safe to adults).

Sulfoxaflor (21.8% SC) is used against Leafhopper (Arboridia vinifera / Empoasca spp.). IRAC Group 4C, mode of action: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor agonist (Systemic). Critical crop stage: Nymph emergence (pre-bloom to post-bloom). Spray timing: Apply when 10–15 nymphs/leaf detected; avoid broad-spectrum flaring mites. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Medium. Rotate with IRAC groups: 9C, 23, 28. Pollinator safety: High Toxicity. Beneficial impact: High Impact.

Deltamethrin (2.8% EC) is used against Tree Cricket (Oecanthus spp.). IRAC Group 3A, mode of action: Sodium channel modulator (Contact). Critical crop stage: Pre-bloom / early shoot growth. Spray timing: Spray late evening (nocturnal feeder); spot-spray borders to preserve beneficials. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Medium. Rotate with IRAC groups: 1B, 28. Pollinator safety: High Toxicity. Beneficial impact: High Impact.

Chlorantraniliprole (18.5% SC) is used against Tobacco Caterpillar (Spodoptera litura). IRAC Group 28, mode of action: Ryanodine receptor modulator (Translaminar / Stomach). Critical crop stage: Early instar larvae (1st–3rd). Spray timing: Apply at 50% egg hatch; use NPV for neonates; avoid late instars. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 4 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: 6, 5, 22A. Pollinator safety: Low. Beneficial impact: Low.

Chlorantraniliprole (18.5% SC) is used against Grapevine Leaf Folder (Sylepta lunalis). IRAC Group 28, mode of action: Ryanodine receptor modulator (Translaminar / Stomach). Critical crop stage: Pre-monsoon (1st generation). Spray timing: Spray when webbing first observed; penetrates folds to reach hidden larvae. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 4 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: 5, 6, 22A. Pollinator safety: Low. Beneficial impact: Low.

Indoxacarb (14.5% SC) is used against Fruit Borer (Helicoverpa armigera). IRAC Group 22A, mode of action: Voltage-gated sodium channel blocker (Contact / Stomach). Critical crop stage: Flowering to berry enlargement. Spray timing: Spray when pheromone traps catch >5 moths/night; target neonates/eggs. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Medium. Rotate with IRAC groups: 28, 6, 5. Pollinator safety: Moderate. Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Chlorantraniliprole (18.5% SC) is used against Grapevine Berry Moth (Lobesia botrana). IRAC Group 28, mode of action: Ryanodine receptor modulator (Translaminar / Stomach). Critical crop stage: Pre-bloom, Post-bloom, Veraison (3 generations). Spray timing: Apply at 50% bloom for 1st gen; repeat at post-bloom & veraison for 2nd/3rd gen. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 4 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: 5, 6, 22A. Pollinator safety: Low. Beneficial impact: Low.

Fipronil (5% SC) [Injection] is used against Grapevine Stem Borer (Celosterna scabrator). IRAC Group 2B, mode of action: GABA-gated chloride channel blocker (Contact / Stomach). Critical crop stage: Adult emergence (summer monsoon). Spray timing: Inject into bore holes & seal with clay; use light traps for mass trapping. Rainfastness: N/A hrs. PHI: N/A days, REI: 24 hrs. Resistance risk: Medium. Rotate with IRAC groups: 3A (trunk paint). Pollinator safety: High Toxicity. Beneficial impact: High Impact.

Metarhizium anisopliae (1.0% WP) is used against Shot Hole Borer (Xylosandrus spp.). IRAC Group UNK (Bio), mode of action: Entomopathogenic fungus (infection) (Contact (spore)). Critical crop stage: Vine stress periods (drought/mechanical damage). Spray timing: Apply as preventive trunk spray; avoid fungicides; maintain vine vigor to deter. Rainfastness: 1–2 hrs. PHI: 0 days, REI: 4 hrs. Resistance risk: Very Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: Azadirachtin (repellent). Pollinator safety: Low. Beneficial impact: Low.

Abamectin (1.9% EC) is used against Red Spider Mite (Tetranychus urticae). IRAC Group 6, mode of action: Glutamate-gated chloride channel modulator (Contact / Stomach). Critical crop stage: Hot, dry spells (March–June). Spray timing: Spray when 5–10 mites/leaf; cover leaf undersides; follow with ovicide in 7 days. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 3 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Medium. Rotate with IRAC groups: 21A, 10B, 23. Pollinator safety: Moderate. Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Abamectin (1.9% EC) is used against Two-spotted Spider Mite (Tetranychus urticae). IRAC Group 6, mode of action: Glutamate-gated chloride channel modulator (Contact / Stomach). Critical crop stage: Same as above. Spray timing: Same as above; reduce dust to prevent flare-ups. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 3 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Medium. Rotate with IRAC groups: 21A, 10B, 23. Pollinator safety: Moderate. Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Hexythiazox (5.45% EC) is used against Yellow Mite (Eotetranychus carpini). IRAC Group 10A, mode of action: Chitin synthesis inhibitor (ovicidal) (Contact). Critical crop stage: Early spring (lower canopy). Spray timing: Apply preventively when mites first appear; excellent ovicidal activity. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: 20D, 21A, 23. Pollinator safety: Moderate. Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Sulphur (80% WG) is used against Rust Mite (Calepitrimerus vitis). IRAC Group UNK (M2), mode of action: Multi-site (contact desiccant) (Contact). Critical crop stage: Bud burst to early shoot growth. Spray timing: Apply at 70% bud break; cover all shoot tips; avoid temps >30°C. Rainfastness: 1–2 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 24 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: Abamectin (6), Fenpyroximate (21A). Pollinator safety: Safe. Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Sulphur (80% WG) [Dormant] is used against Bud Mite (Colomerus vitis). IRAC Group UNK (M2), mode of action: Multi-site (contact desiccant) (Contact). Critical crop stage: Dormant (post-pruning) & Green-tip stage. Spray timing: Apply dormant sulfur + oil to kill overwintering mites in bud scales; remove galled buds. Rainfastness: 1–2 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 24 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: Abamectin (6). Pollinator safety: Safe. Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Fluopyram (34.48% SC) is used against Root-knot Nematode (Meloidogyne incognita). IRAC Group 7 (Nematicide), mode of action: SDHI (mitochondrial complex II) (Systemic (soil drench)). Critical crop stage: Pre-planting or early post-plant (root flush). Spray timing: Apply as drip drench during active root growth (spring/monsoon). Rainfastness: N/A hrs. PHI: 30+ days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: Fluensulfone, Cyclobutrifluoram. Pollinator safety: Safe. Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Fluopyram (34.48% SC) is used against Citrus Nematode (Tylenchulus semipenetrans). IRAC Group 7 (Nematicide), mode of action: SDHI (Systemic (soil drench)). Critical crop stage: Pre-planting or early root flush. Spray timing: Soil drench to dripline; combine with Paecilomyces lilacinus (bio) for organic integration. Rainfastness: N/A hrs. PHI: 30+ days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: Fluensulfone. Pollinator safety: Safe. Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Fluensulfone (2% GR) is used against Reniform Nematode (Rotylenchulus reniformis). IRAC Group UNK, mode of action: Nematicide (fumigant-like) (Contact (soil)). Critical crop stage: Pre-planting or root flush (pre-monsoon). Spray timing: Incorporate into 15–30 cm root zone via drip irrigation; focus on light-textured soils. Rainfastness: N/A hrs. PHI: 30 days, REI: 48 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: Fluopyram, Cyclobutrifluoram. Pollinator safety: Safe. Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Metaldehyde (2.5% DP) is used against Snails (Various spp.). IRAC Group UNK, mode of action: Molluscicide (stomach poison) (Stomach (bait)). Critical crop stage: Post-rainfall periods (monsoon). Spray timing: Apply baits in early morning/evening before rain; use bait traps for monitoring. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: Copper barriers (M1). Pollinator safety: Safe (but toxic to pets). Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Metaldehyde (2.5% DP) is used against Slugs (Various spp.). IRAC Group UNK, mode of action: Molluscicide (stomach poison) (Stomach (bait)). Critical crop stage: Monsoon/wet periods (twilight). Spray timing: Apply to soil surface near low-hanging clusters; remove leaf litter; use copper trunk barriers. Rainfastness: 2–4 hrs. PHI: 7 days, REI: 12 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: Copper Hydroxide barriers. Pollinator safety: Safe. Beneficial impact: Moderate.

Physical Exclusion (Nets) is used against Birds (Various spp.). IRAC Group N/A, mode of action: Physical barrier (N/A). Critical crop stage: Veraison (berry coloring) to harvest. Spray timing: Install 20–25mm mesh nets 2–3 weeks pre-veraison; secure at bottom. Rainfastness: N/A hrs. PHI: N/A days, REI: N/A hrs. Resistance risk: N/A. Rotate with IRAC groups: Rotate scare devices (acoustic/visual). Pollinator safety: Safe. Beneficial impact: Safe.

Physical Exclusion (Nets/Flashing Lights) is used against Fruit Bats (Pteropus spp.). IRAC Group N/A, mode of action: Physical barrier / Visual deterrent (N/A). Critical crop stage: Veraison to harvest (nighttime). Spray timing: Drape 30mm monofilament nets; combine with ultrasonic devices & flashing lights. Rainfastness: N/A hrs. PHI: N/A days, REI: N/A hrs. Resistance risk: N/A. Rotate with IRAC groups: Harvest early to remove attractant. Pollinator safety: Safe. Beneficial impact: Safe.

Brodifacoum (0.005% BB) / Zinc Phosphide (80% Powder) is used against Rodents (Rats / Mice). IRAC Group N/A, mode of action: Anticoagulant / Acute toxicant (Stomach (bait)). Critical crop stage: Dormant season (winter). Spray timing: Place fresh bait in secure stations (10–15m spacing) during dormancy; avoid pre-harvest placement. Rainfastness: N/A hrs. PHI: N/A days, REI: 48 hrs. Resistance risk: Low. Rotate with IRAC groups: Sanitation (weed/wood removal). Pollinator safety: High Toxicity (non-target). Beneficial impact: High Impact.

Downy mildew is the most destructive grape disease in wet, humid climates. The pathogen requires 4–6 hours of leaf wetness at 15–25°C for infection. Use protective fungicides (Mancozeb/Copper) before forecasted rain, and penetrant fungicides (Metalaxyl, Cymoxanil, Dimethomorph) within 72 hours post-infection for kick-back activity. Resistance to FRAC 4 (Metalaxyl) and FRAC 11 (QoI) is widespread—rotate with FRAC 40, 27, and M3. Canopy management (shoot positioning, leaf removal) is critical to reduce leaf wetness duration. PHI: Mancozeb 66 days; others 7–14 days. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Oomycete. Key registered chemicals: Mancozeb 75% WP (M3), Copper Hydroxide 77% WP (M1), Cymoxanil 50% WP (27), Dimethomorph 50% WP (40), Metalaxyl-M 31.8% ES (4), Fosetyl-Al 80% WP (P07), Azoxystrobin 23% SC (11), Mandipropamid 23.4% SC (40), Cyazofamid 34.5% SC (21). Critical spray timing: Pre-bloom through 6–8 weeks post-bloom; apply protectively before rain events..

Powdery mildew thrives in warm (20–27°C), humid conditions but does NOT require free water—it infects in dry conditions. Sulphur is the most cost-effective protectant, but do not apply above 30°C (phytotoxicity risk). For curative action, use DMIs (FRAC 3) within 72 hours of infection, but DMI resistance is common—rotate with FRAC 50 (Metrafenone) and FRAC 11. Early season control (bud break to bloom) is critical to prevent berry infection. Canopy opening (leaf removal around clusters) reduces humidity and disease pressure. PHI: Sulphur 7–14 days; DMIs 7–21 days. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Fungus. Key registered chemicals: Sulphur 80% WG (M2), Lime Sulphur 22% SC (M2), Tebuconazole 25.9% EC (3), Difenoconazole 25% EC (3), Hexaconazole 5% EC (3), Propiconazole 25% EC (3), Azoxystrobin 23% SC (11), Metrafenone 500 g/L SC (50), Myclobutanil 10% WP (3). Critical spray timing: Pre-bloom through 2–3 weeks post-bloom; protect for 4–6 weeks..

Anthracnose causes characteristic "bird's-eye" lesions on leaves, shoots, and berries. The fungus overwinters in infected canes and mummified berries. Dormant lime sulfur (1–2 weeks before bud break) is the most effective single treatment. During the growing season, protect young tissues with Mancozeb or Captan starting at 4–10 inch shoot growth. Wet, warm conditions favor disease spread; reapply after heavy rain. Copper is effective but can cause phytotoxicity on certain varieties. Remove and destroy infected plant material during pruning. PHI: Mancozeb 66 days; Captan 3–7 days. REI: 24 hours. Category: Fungus. Key registered chemicals: Mancozeb 75% WP (M3), Captan 50% WP (M4), Copper Hydroxide 77% WP (M1), Lime Sulphur 22% SC (M2), Difenoconazole 25% EC (3), Carbendazim 50% WP (1), Thiophanate-methyl 70% WP (1). Critical spray timing: Dormant (lime sulfur) and early shoot growth (4–10 inch shoots); repeat at 10–14 day intervals..

Botrytis is a necrotrophic fungus that infects flowers, then remains latent until berry ripening. Tight-clustered varieties are most susceptible. Bloom application is essential to prevent latent infections—use FRAC 2 (Iprodione) or FRAC 12 (Fludioxonil). Pre-harvest sprays (veraison) protect ripening berries; FRAC 17 (Fenhexamid) and FRAC 9 (Cyprodinil) are effective but resistance is common. Resistance to FRAC 2, 7, and 9 is widespread—rotate with multi-site M3/M4 fungicides. Canopy management (cluster thinning, leaf removal) and avoiding wounding are critical cultural controls. PHI: 7–14 days. REI: 12 hours. Category: Fungus. Key registered chemicals: Captan 50% WP (M4), Iprodione 50% WP (2), Fludioxonil 20.4% SC (12), Thiophanate-methyl 70% WP (1), Carbendazim 50% WP (1), Ziram 80% WP (M3), Thiram 80% WP (M3). Critical spray timing: Critical: Bloom (flower parts) and pre-harvest (berry ripening)..

Black Rot causes "mummified" berries that can lead to complete crop loss. The fungus requires 6–12 hours of wetness at 20–28°C for infection. Protective fungicides (Mancozeb) must be applied before infection periods. DMIs (FRAC 3) and QoIs (FRAC 11) provide excellent curative activity up to 72 hours post-infection. Captan and Copper are ineffective against Black Rot—do not rely on them. Sanitation is critical: remove and destroy mummified berries from the vineyard and trellis wires during winter. Resistance to FRAC 11 is reported—rotate with FRAC 3 and M3. PHI: Mancozeb 66 days; DMIs 7–21 days. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Fungus. Key registered chemicals: Mancozeb 75% WP (M3), Difenoconazole 25% EC (3), Propiconazole 25% EC (3), Tebuconazole 25.9% EC (3), Azoxystrobin 23% SC (11), Myclobutanil 10% WP (3), Dithianon 75% WP (M9). Critical spray timing: Immediate pre-bloom through 2–3 weeks post-bloom; protect young berries..

Phomopsis causes cane bleaching, leaf spots, and berry rot. The fungus overwinters in infected canes and requires water for spore germination in cool conditions (8–15°C). Early season protection is essential—apply Mancozeb or Captan starting at 1–2 inch shoot growth and continue through bloom. Dormant lime sulfur (pre-bud break) reduces inoculum. No curative fungicides are available—all sprays must be protective. Remove infected canes during pruning to reduce primary inoculum. The disease takes 4–5 years to become noticeable; prevention is the only strategy. PHI: Mancozeb 66 days; Captan 3–7 days. REI: 24 hours. Category: Fungus. Key registered chemicals: Mancozeb 75% WP (M3), Captan 50% WP (M4), Ziram 80% WP (M3), Carbendazim 50% WP (1), Thiophanate-methyl 70% WP (1). Critical spray timing: Start at 1–2 inch shoot length; repeat at 7–10 day intervals depending on rain..

Alternaria causes brown concentric leaf spots and premature defoliation, especially in warm, humid conditions. The fungus is a weak pathogen that typically attacks stressed or senescing tissues. Protective fungicides (Mancozeb/Captan) applied for other diseases usually provide adequate control. If severe, add QoI (Azoxystrobin) or DMI (Difenoconazole) for enhanced activity. Sanitation—removing infected leaf litter—reduces overwintering inoculum. Maintain vine vigor through proper irrigation and nutrition to reduce susceptibility. This disease is rarely a primary target; control is usually achieved through multi-purpose fungicide programs. PHI: Mancozeb 66 days; Captan 3–7 days. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Fungus. Key registered chemicals: Mancozeb 75% WP (M3), Captan 50% WP (M4), Copper Hydroxide 77% WP (M1), Azoxystrobin 23% SC (11), Difenoconazole 25% EC (3). Critical spray timing: Early to mid-season; apply when symptoms first appear..

Cercospora causes small brown to gray leaf lesions, primarily on older leaves near the vineyard floor. It is favored by warm, humid conditions and is generally a minor disease in well-managed vineyards. Mancozeb or Copper sprays applied for Downy Mildew usually provide suppression. In severe cases, Chlorothalonil (FRAC M5) is effective. Canopy management—opening the canopy and improving air circulation—reduces disease pressure. Leaf litter removal in winter reduces primary inoculum. Focus on overall vine health; the disease rarely causes economic damage if other diseases are controlled. PHI: Mancozeb 66 days; Chlorothalonil 7–14 days. REI: 24 hours. Category: Fungus. Key registered chemicals: Mancozeb 75% WP (M3), Copper Hydroxide 77% WP (M1), Chlorothalonil 75% WP (M5). Critical spray timing: Mid to late season; apply when symptoms appear..

Rust causes orange to brown pustules on leaf undersides, leading to premature defoliation and reduced photosynthesis. The fungus requires free water for spore germination and is favored by warm (20–30°C), humid conditions. Protective fungicides (Mancozeb/Copper) applied for Downy Mildew provide suppression. For active infections, use QoI (Azoxystrobin) or DMI (Tebuconazole) for curative activity. Resistance to QoIs is reported—rotate with DMIs and multi-site fungicides. Remove infected leaves and improve canopy airflow. This disease is more common in humid tropical regions and can be severe if left unmanaged. PHI: Mancozeb 66 days; DMIs 7–21 days. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Fungus. Key registered chemicals: Mancozeb 75% WP (M3), Copper Hydroxide 77% WP (M1), Azoxystrobin 23% SC (11), Tebuconazole 25.9% EC (3). Critical spray timing: Early to mid-season; apply when orange pustules appear on leaf undersides..

Dead Arm causes dieback of shoots and canes, with wedge-shaped wood discoloration. The fungi enter through pruning wounds, making wound protection the primary control strategy. Apply Copper-based or Mancozeb sprays immediately after pruning to seal wounds. Remove and destroy all dead or dying canes during pruning to reduce inoculum. Avoid pruning during wet weather to minimize spore dispersal. Maintain vine vigor through balanced nutrition and irrigation. There are no curative treatments for infected wood—prevention through wound protection and sanitation is essential. PHI: Not applicable for dormant sprays. REI: 24 hours. Category: Fungus (Trunk Disease). Key registered chemicals: No direct chemical control; preventive: Copper Hydroxide (M1) (dormant), Mancozeb (M3) (post-pruning). Critical spray timing: Dormant (post-pruning); apply to pruning wounds to prevent infection..

Eutypa causes stunted shoots and wedge-shaped wood discoloration, leading to gradual vine decline. The fungus enters through pruning wounds and can take years to show symptoms. Wound protection with Copper-based paints or Thiophanate-methyl immediately after pruning is the only chemical strategy. Prune during dry weather and make clean cuts at the cordon to minimize infection sites. Remove and burn infected arms—do not compost them. There is no cure for infected vines; prevention through wound protection and sanitation is critical. In severely affected vineyards, consider replanting with resistant rootstocks. PHI: Not applicable. REI: 24 hours. Category: Fungus (Trunk Disease). Key registered chemicals: No registered chemical cure; preventive: Copper (M1), Thiophanate-methyl (1) (wound protectants). Critical spray timing: Dormant (post-pruning); protect pruning wounds immediately..

Esca is a complex trunk disease causing leaf striping, berry spotting, and vine decline. The fungi enter through pruning wounds and spread through the vascular system. No curative fungicides are available. Management focuses on prevention: protect pruning wounds with Copper-based paints; remove and destroy symptomatic vines. Fosetyl-Al foliar sprays may improve vine health but do not cure the disease. Avoid water stress and maintain balanced nutrition to support vine defenses. Remove infected wood during pruning and seal wounds. In severe cases, replant affected blocks with clean planting material. PHI: Not applicable. REI: 24 hours. Category: Fungus (Trunk Disease). Key registered chemicals: No direct chemical control; preventive: Copper (M1) (dormant), Fosetyl-Al (P07) (foliar). Critical spray timing: Dormant (wound protection) and growing season (foliar supportive)..

Armillaria causes root decay, wilting, and vine death, often in a characteristic "ring" pattern in the vineyard. The fungus survives for decades on dead roots in the soil. Pre-plant soil fumigation with methyl bromide (now restricted) or soil solarization are the only chemical options. Cultural controls: remove all root debris from previous plantings; use resistant rootstocks (e.g., Vitis berlandieri hybrids); avoid planting in known infested sites. Once established, there is no cure—remove and destroy infected vines and roots. Irrigation management—avoid overwatering—reduces fungal spread. PHI: Not applicable. REI: 48+ hours for fumigants. Category: Fungus (Root Disease). Key registered chemicals: No registered chemical control; soil fumigation (pre-plant). Critical spray timing: Pre-planting (site preparation)..

Fusarium causes root rot and poor vine growth, especially in stressed or waterlogged soils. The fungus is widespread in soil and infects through root wounds. Carbendazim or Thiophanate-methyl soil drenches may provide suppression but are not curative. Prevention is key: plant on well-drained soils; avoid over-irrigation; use resistant rootstocks; rotate with non-host crops before replanting. Organic matter (compost) incorporation improves soil health and suppresses Fusarium. Remove and destroy severely infected vines. PHI: 30+ days for soil treatments. REI: 24 hours. Category: Fungus (Root Disease). Key registered chemicals: No direct chemical control; soil drench: Carbendazim 50% WP (1) (limited). Critical spray timing: Pre-planting or early post-plant (soil treatment)..

Rhizoctonia causes root decay and damping-off in young vines. The fungus thrives in warm, moist soils and infects through root wounds. Carboxin (FRAC 7) seed/rootstock treatments provide protection against Rhizoctonia. Cultural controls: plant on well-drained soils; avoid planting too deep; manage irrigation to prevent waterlogging. Crop rotation before replanting reduces soil inoculum. Biological controls (Trichoderma spp.) can be incorporated into the planting hole to suppress the pathogen. Remove infected vines and solarize the soil before replanting. PHI: Not applicable for pre-plant treatments. REI: 12 hours. Category: Fungus (Root Disease). Key registered chemicals: No direct chemical control; seed treatment: Carboxin 75% WP (7) (for rootstocks). Critical spray timing: Pre-planting (rootstock treatment) or early post-plant..

Crown Gall causes tumor-like galls on trunks and crowns, disrupting vascular function. The bacterium enters through wounds (pruning cuts, frost cracks, grafting sites). No chemical cure exists—prevention is the only strategy. Biological control using Agrobacterium radiobacter strain K84 (a non-pathogenic strain) is highly effective—apply as a dip to rootstocks or as a wound dressing immediately after pruning. Avoid wounding vines during cultivation. Remove and destroy galled vines; do not replant in the same site for 3–5 years. Copper sprays on pruning wounds provide some protection but are less effective than biologicals. PHI: Not applicable. REI: 12 hours. Category: Bacterium. Key registered chemicals: No curative chemical; preventive: Copper Hydroxide (M1) (dormant), biological control (Agrobacterium radiobacter K84). Critical spray timing: Dormant (post-pruning); apply to pruning wounds..

Pierce's Disease causes leaf scorch, berry shrivel, and vine decline. The bacterium is transmitted by xylem-feeding insects (leafhoppers, sharpshooters). No curative treatment exists for infected vines—remove and destroy them. Management focuses on vector control: use IRAC 4A (Imidacloprid) or IRAC 4C (Sulfoxaflor) to reduce vector populations. Remove infected vines promptly to prevent spread. Resistant rootstocks and varieties are the only long-term solution. In areas with high disease pressure, continuous vector monitoring and timely insecticide applications are essential. PHI: 7–14 days for insecticides. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Bacterium. Key registered chemicals: No curative chemical; preventive: insecticides for vector control (leafhoppers). Critical spray timing: Throughout growing season; target insect vectors (leafhoppers, sharpshooters)..

Bacterial Leaf Spot causes water-soaked to necrotic lesions on leaves, often in warm, wet conditions. Copper-based bactericides (FRAC M1) are the primary chemical control—apply protectively before rain events. Streptomycin + Tetracycline combination provides systemic activity but resistance is a concern—limit use. Cultural controls: avoid overhead irrigation; improve canopy airflow; remove infected leaf litter in winter. Copper resistance in Xanthomonas populations is increasing—rotate copper with biological or other bactericides. Sanitation—removing infected plant material—is critical for long-term management. PHI: Copper 1–14 days; Streptomycin 14–21 days. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Bacterium. Key registered chemicals: Copper Hydroxide 77% WP (M1), Copper Oxychloride 50% WP (M1), Copper Sulphate (M1), Streptomycin + Tetracycline (9%+1%). Critical spray timing: Early season; apply before rain events when temperatures are warm..

Fanleaf causes fan-shaped leaves, poor fruit set, and reduced yield. The virus is transmitted by the dagger nematode (Xiphinema index). No chemical cure exists for infected vines—remove and destroy them. Management focuses on nematode control: pre-plant soil fumigation or Fluopyram/Fluensulfone applications to reduce vector populations. Use virus-tested planting material—this is the most critical control measure. In infected vineyards, rogue (remove) symptomatic vines immediately. Do not replant with susceptible varieties in infested soil without nematode control. PHI: 30+ days for nematicides. REI: 24–48 hours. Category: Virus. Key registered chemicals: No chemical control. Vector control: Nematicides for nematode vectors (Fluopyram 34.48% SC, Fluensulfone 2% GR). Critical spray timing: Pre-planting (soil treatment for nematode vectors) and early season (vector control)..

Leafroll causes downward leaf rolling, discoloration, and delayed ripening. The virus is transmitted by mealybugs (Planococcus spp.) and scale insects. No chemical cure exists—remove infected vines. Management focuses on mealybug control: use Spirotetramat (IRAC 23) or Buprofezin (IRAC 16) to suppress vector populations. Use virus-tested planting material—this is the only reliable prevention. Rouge (remove) symptomatic vines immediately to prevent spread. Control ants that protect mealybugs. In severely affected blocks, consider complete replanting with certified virus-free material. PHI: 7–14 days for insecticides. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Virus. Key registered chemicals: No chemical control. Vector control: Imidacloprid (IRAC 4A), Buprofezin (IRAC 16) (for mealybug vectors). Critical spray timing: Early season to post-harvest; target mealybug vectors..

Fleck Virus causes mild chlorosis and is often symptomless on many cultivars. The virus is transmitted by soilborne vectors (unknown) and through propagation material. No chemical control exists—management relies entirely on using virus-tested planting material. The disease is generally of minor economic importance unless co-infected with other viruses. Do not propagate from infected vines. There is no vector control strategy because the vector is unknown. Focus on sanitation and using certified virus-free rootstocks and scions. Remove severely affected vines if yield decline is observed. PHI: Not applicable. REI: Not applicable. Category: Virus. Key registered chemicals: No chemical control.. Critical spray timing: Not applicable (no chemical control)..

Rugose Wood causes stem grooving and reduced vigor. The viruses are transmitted through propagation material and possibly by mealybugs. No chemical cure exists—management relies on virus-tested planting material and sanitation. Rouge (remove) symptomatic vines immediately to prevent spread. The disease is often asymptomatic on some rootstocks but can cause severe decline on others. Do not use infected material for grafting or propagation. In nurseries, heat treatment of propagation material may reduce virus titers but does not eliminate the virus. PHI: Not applicable. REI: Not applicable. Category: Virus. Key registered chemicals: No chemical control.. Critical spray timing: Not applicable (no chemical control)..

Red Blotch causes red blotches on leaves and delayed ripening, severely impacting berry quality. The virus is transmitted by treehoppers and spittlebugs. No chemical cure exists—remove infected vines. Vector control using IRAC 4A (Imidacloprid) or IRAC 4C (Sulfoxaflor) can reduce secondary spread. Use virus-tested planting material—this is the only reliable prevention. Rouge (remove) symptomatic vines immediately. The virus can take 2–3 years to show symptoms; regular monitoring is essential. In severely affected blocks, complete replanting with certified virus-free material is recommended. PHI: 7–14 days for insecticides. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Virus. Key registered chemicals: No chemical control. Vector control: insecticides for treehoppers/spittlebugs (Imidacloprid, IRAC 4A). Critical spray timing: Early season to post-harvest; target insect vectors..

Bois Noir causes yellowing, poor fruit set, and shoot abnormalities. The phytoplasma is transmitted by leafhoppers (Hyalesthes obsoletus). No chemical cure exists—remove infected vines. Management focuses on vector control: use IRAC 4A (Imidacloprid) or IRAC 3A (Cypermethrin) to reduce leafhopper populations. Weed management (removing host plants like bindweed) reduces vector breeding sites. Use clean planting material. In high-pressure areas, insecticide applications during vector flight periods (spring/summer) are essential. Rouge (remove) symptomatic vines promptly. PHI: 7–14 days for insecticides. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Phytoplasma. Key registered chemicals: No direct chemical control. Vector control: insecticides for leafhoppers (IRAC 4A, 3A, 1B). Critical spray timing: Early season (vector emergence); target leafhopper vectors..

Flavescence Dorée causes yellowing, leaf rolling, and bunch drying. This is a regulated quarantine pest in many regions—mandatory control measures apply. The phytoplasma is transmitted by the leafhopper Scaphoideus titanus. No chemical cure exists—remove infected vines immediately. Mandatory insecticide treatments (IRAC 4A, 3A, or 1B) are required in affected areas to control the vector. Two to three insecticide applications are typically required during the vector's life cycle. Rouge (remove) all symptomatic vines; in severe cases, entire blocks may need to be removed. Use certified clean planting material. PHI: 7–14 days for insecticides. REI: 12–24 hours. Category: Phytoplasma. Key registered chemicals: No direct chemical control. Vector control: insecticides for leafhoppers (IRAC 4A, 3A, 1B). Critical spray timing: Early season (vector emergence); mandatory insecticide treatments in regulated areas..

Sooty Mold is a black fungal growth on leaves and berries, feeding on honeydew excreted by sap-sucking insects (mealybugs, aphids, whiteflies, scale). The mold itself does not infect the plant—it reduces photosynthesis and fruit quality. Control the underlying insect pest using appropriate insecticides (IRAC 4A, 23, 16, 7C). Wash off honeydew and sooty mold with high-pressure water jets if feasible. Ant control is critical because ants protect honeydew-producing insects. Monitor for insect infestations regularly and treat early. PHI: Follow insecticide PHI. REI: Follow insecticide REI. Category: Secondary Fungus. Key registered chemicals: No direct fungicide; control the honeydew-producing insects (Mealybugs, Aphids, Whiteflies, Scale). Critical spray timing: Not applicable (treat underlying pest infestation)..
